Requires exact matching against an explicit value set
Requires one shared predicate rather than copy-pasted matchers
Requires an audit trail of auto-excluded rows so a wrong suppression is visible

evals.prompt: We probed an external dataset for a distress/liveness signal: the API works, the schema has the right per-entity metrics, and ~13% of our targets match host-exact. Greenlight building the classifier and scoring on it?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- API-works, has-the-fields, and adequate match-rate can all be green while the data is silently months stale, describing last year's state instead of current. Before building a current-state signal, query the MAX timestamp per metric (per-metric, since columns in one table lag differently) and compare to today; if the newest sample lags many months, the signal is real but describes the past, and the decision flips from 'build and wire it' to 'keep a re-runnable probe + route the revisit to the owner.' Label any derived signal by the recency of the metric it is actually computed from, not the freshest column. Run the cheapest decisive go/no-go query first -- freshness, not match-rate, was the real kill-question. The probe itself is the deliverable. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires a max-timestamp / freshness check per metric before greenlighting a current-state signal
Does not accept API-works + schema + match-rate as sufficient feasibility
Labels a derived signal by the recency of the metric it is computed from
Treats the re-runnable probe (and a 'too stale' finding) as the valuable deliverable

evals.prompt: Our no-regressions check flags this PR because a settings section that used to be a top-level nav item is now nested under a new 'Admin' parent. Is that a removed feature to block on?
evals.expected_output: No -- a moved feature is not a removed one. A destructive-change gate that keys on surface position (a top-level nav slot, a route path) false-fires on a legitimate reorganisation, and -- worse -- a label-presence check misses a genuinely orphaned route (still in the menu, reachable by nobody). Key the invariant on REACHABILITY over the before-vs-after route/navigation graph: every prior capability still reachable through some path, with its history preserved, is not a regression no matter where it now sits; a capability reachable by no path IS a regression no matter what label lingers. Relocation is not removal, and a stable label is not proof of reachability. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not treat a relocated (still-reachable) feature as a removed feature
Computes the no-regression invariant over the route/navigation reachability graph, not nav-position stability
Still catches a genuinely orphaned/unreachable route despite a lingering label

evals.prompt: Our deploy build timed out with a 504, but /health still returns 200, so the new version is live -- right?
evals.expected_output: No -- /health cannot confirm a promotion when both the old and new artifact answer it. On a build-then-promote platform the OLD pod keeps returning /health = 200 throughout a slow build's 504, so polling it 'proves' a success that never happened (the old artifact answering). Pick a DISCRIMINATOR that differs between the artifacts and poll that: a static asset path the new build ships and the old lacked (404 -> 200 exactly when the new pod takes over), a build/commit id, or a changed response header. A response byte only the new build can serve is the honest promotion signal; verify by that effect, not a liveness endpoint both builds produce. (infra-iac-containers.md.)
expectations: Rejects /health = 200 as proof the new build was promoted
Explains that the old pod can keep answering /health during a slow build's timeout
Requires polling a discriminator only the new build serves (new asset path, build id, changed header)

evals.prompt: We want to add a 'confirmed by N sources' badge and an X% match-confidence to our provenance UI. Build it?
evals.expected_output: Measure the field's distribution on real data first -- even a tier is false precision if the signal is near-constant. If corroborationCount is 1 on almost every row (e.g. 16,008 of 16,012), a 'confirmed by N sources' badge fires on a fraction of a percent of rows and reads '1 source' everywhere else; if match-confidence is 0.9 on ~70% and 0.8 on the rest, it is effectively binary and 'X% confidence' manufactures precision the pipeline lacks. If the field barely varies, showing it is false precision, not transparency -- drop it or reframe to something that actually varies (how an entity was matched, not a number). A misleading signal is worse than an honest blank (empty beats fabricated). (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires measuring the actual field distribution before designing the confidence/corroboration display
Treats a near-constant field shown as a confidence/corroboration signal as false precision
Recommends dropping or reframing to a signal that actually varies (how matched, not a number)
Invokes empty-beats-fabricated: a misleading signal is worse than an honest blank

evals.prompt: Our verify pipeline is a standalone typecheck then a build (the build has typescript.ignoreBuildErrors, so it doesn't re-check types), and it's green on a fresh clone in CI. But a teammate says tsc fails when they re-run it locally. Is CI's green enough?
evals.expected_output: No -- prove the gate idempotent by running it twice, not just green from a clean clone. A gate whose steps write artifacts a later step consumes can pass once and fail on the next run against what the first run generated: here the build emits generated route types (.next/types/**) that a subsequent standalone tsc --noEmit then rejects, so a clean-clone CI run never sees it while the local re-run hits a confusing red -- the gate is order-dependent, not flaky. Run it twice (or clean the generated dirs first) and treat the second-run failure as a real finding. One concrete trigger: a non-handler export (a helper/constant/classifier) from a framework route module (a Next.js App Router route.ts) makes the generated validator reject the module -- move the pure logic to a sibling module. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not accept green-from-a-clean-clone as proof; requires running the gate twice (or cleaning generated dirs)
Identifies an order-dependent gate where a build writes artifacts a later step consumes
Flags a non-handler export from a framework route module and moves pure logic to a sibling
Treats the second-run failure as a real finding, not flakiness

evals.prompt: We keep a brand-grey token below AA on purpose ('decorative only') and a unit test asserts its value stays sub-AA. Good enough to prove it's accessible?
evals.expected_output: No -- that test pins the wrong end. It proves the token's value stays decorative; it never proves no component paints real, informational TEXT with it. WCAG 1.4.3 holds informational text to 4.5:1 (large text 3:1), so a className/style that colours a visible label, status word, or helper line with the decorative token fails the audit on every route sharing that chrome, while the value-only test stays green (the fast tier can't see it; only the browser/a11y gate can). Add a lint/test that fails when the token colours a real text node -- fail-closed, but with an escape: admit a pinned a11y-exempt marker for text 1.4.3 genuinely exempts (aria-hidden or purely-decorative glyphs, logotypes, large text meeting 3:1), so the gate is narrowed to the standard, not stricter than it. Allow the token freely on non-text (borders, backgrounds, icon fills with an accessible-name sibling), and plant both a real-text use (guard fires) and a pinned-exempt use (guard stays silent). Assert the usage constraint, not just the value. Generally: when a test encodes an intent ('stays decorative', 'stays internal', 'never renders'), verify the property, not the value it is derived from. (frontend-a11y.md.)
expectations: Rejects a value-only test as proof the decorative token is accessible
Requires a use-site guard that fails when the token colors a text node
Guards real text use but admits a pinned-exempt marker for genuinely-decorative / aria-hidden / logotype text, so the gate is not stricter than SC 1.4.3
Generalizes to asserting the property, not the value it is derived from

evals.prompt: The browser suite OOM-killed at the default worker count, so I ran it with --workers=1 and two specs failed. Should I file those as regressions?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- classify by config and baseline first. Cutting workers to fit memory changes the execution model, not just speed: serial specs sharing one stateful backend can pollute a later spec's precondition, so a failure seen ONLY under --workers=1 can be a harness artifact the sharded CI config never hits, not a product regression. The mirror error is as easy -- a change can genuinely make a suite serial-fragile -- so 'it's just --workers=1' is also unverified. Two cheap runs: (config axis) reproduce the suspect specs under CI's actual worker config (a few specs won't OOM) -- pass there and it is not a gate failure; (baseline axis) run them under the identical reduced config on the merge-base -- pass-baseline + fail-branch is a real code-introduced sensitivity, fail-both is a pre-existing harness artifact. Report which config and which baseline the failure belongs to; 'fails under --workers=1 locally' and 'fails the gate CI runs' are different findings. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not report a --workers=1-only failure as a regression without classifying it
Reproduces the suspect specs under CI's actual (parallel) worker config as the config axis
Runs the identical reduced config on the merge-base as the baseline axis
Names which config and which baseline the failure belongs to

evals.prompt: Our differ confirmed every element and control in the design is present in the app, so we signed off parity. (The app also renders an extra header, view tabs, a filter bar, a 'Showing N of N' line, and per-card upvote arrows the design doesn't have -- but those are intentional extra functionality.) Good?
evals.expected_output: No -- that checked only one direction (design subset of app) and missed the other (app subset of design). Visual parity is SET EQUALITY, not containment: an element present on exactly one side is a finding regardless of which side, and 'intentional extra functionality' is the rationalization that ships the mismatch. Diff both ways per screen, list what the app renders that the design doesn't, then apply the operative test to each app-only item -- does removing it lose a user capability? Pure shell loses none: the extra header and the 'Showing N of N' line default to remove-to-match. Capability-bearing chrome IS a feature, not a bonus: the view tabs (navigating), the filter bar (filtering), and the per-card upvote arrows (upvoting) each is a feature to RESTYLE into the target's design language (re-express the capability in the reference's own primitives) so the look reaches parity while the capability is preserved -- never self-cut to match, and deleting app-only functionality to reach parity without a named owner approval is a High do-no-harm finding; escalate to the owner only as a fallback when no target primitive fits (migration-parity's restyle-an-app-only-feature rule). Scope this to chrome/features; data (values, counts, series) legitimately differs. Sign-off needs the design->app list empty and the app->design list empty or every entry resolved -- restyled into the target language, decoration removed, or an owner-adjudicated keep/removal. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects a one-directional (design subset of app) check; requires diffing app->design too
Applies the operative test -- does removing an app-only element lose a user capability?
Classifies the filter bar, view tabs, and per-card upvote arrows as capability-bearing features to restyle into the target design language, not shell to delete
Removes pure shell (extra header, 'Showing N of N' line) to match, but restyles features into the target design language (escalating only as a fallback) rather than deleting or self-certifying

evals.prompt: We're porting the app to a design mockup. The app has a filter bar and a per-row action menu the mockup doesn't show. To reach visual parity a reviewer proposes deleting both. There's no owner sign-off on dropping them. What's the correct call?
evals.expected_output: Don't delete them to match a look reference -- a mockup is a look reference, not a feature spec. Classify each app-only element by the operative test: does removing it lose a user capability? The filter bar (filtering) and the action menu (its actions) are real functionality, so the deliverable is to RESTYLE them into the target's design language -- re-express each capability in the reference's own primitives (its button, its menu, its filter control) so the look reaches parity while the capability is preserved. That is what 'preserve' means here: preserve the capability, not leave it in the old visual language and not escalate-and-wait. Deleting app-only functionality to reach parity without a named owner approval is a High do-no-harm finding -- it blocks unless a named owner accepts the loss (that acceptance is the only path that removes a real feature). Only pure decoration (an extra header, a count line) removes-to-match; escalation to the owner is the fallback when no target primitive fits. Fill the exception ledger -- element, bucket (decoration/functionality/owner-approved), verdict, target primitive -- before implementing, so nothing is silently deleted. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Rejects deleting the filter bar and action menu to match the mockup
Prescribes restyling the real features into the target's design language, preserving the capability
Names deleting app-only functionality without a named owner approval as a High do-no-harm finding (blocks unless an owner accepts)
Requires classifying each app-only element (decoration / functionality / owner-approved) via the exception ledger before implementing, citing migration-parity.md

evals.prompt: I'm reviewing a visual restyle a write lane committed in its own worktree (branch feat/restyle). A dev server is already running on http://localhost:3000 -- but it was launched from the owner's own checkout, which is on main and never pulled feat/restyle. Can I tell the owner 'the restyle is live, open localhost:3000 to see it'?
evals.expected_output: No. That URL is serving the owner's tree (main), not the tree under review (feat/restyle) -- the change never rendered there, so 'it's live, open localhost:3000' is a claim about the wrong surface: true about your branch, false on every surface the owner can open. Name the verification surface explicitly -- url-or-port, tree/worktree path, branch, and the sha actually rendered (the VERIFY_SURFACE field) -- and flag that the served tree is NOT the tree under review. Do not say 'it's live' or 'check it locally' until you have served feat/restyle yourself (its own worktree/build) or confirmed the served sha equals feat/restyle's head, the way a deploy is confirmed -- by fetching a byte only the new build serves, not by assuming a rebuild happened. A parity claim that names no URL and no rendered sha is invalid, not merely downgraded. (report-format.md.)
expectations: Refuses to tell the owner 'it's live / check localhost:3000' while the served tree is main, not feat/restyle
Requires naming the surface (url-or-port, tree/worktree, branch, sha actually rendered) and flagging that the served tree is not the tree under review
Requires serving the change's tree or confirming served-sha equals feat/restyle head (deploy-confirmation style) before any live claim
States a parity claim naming no URL and no sha is invalid, not downgraded, citing report-format.md

evals.prompt: Mirroring an approved design into our app. From a cropped screenshot of the design, I see the app has a stepper with up/down arrows the design doesn't show, and the app is missing a 'filters' control the design has. I'm about to remove the stepper and add a filters control to reach parity. Right?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- a cropped screenshot of one side is a hypothesis, not evidence, and every 'extra'/'missing' call here is one destructive edit away. Before claiming either delta, render BOTH sides at the same viewport width and diff the corresponding region directly. Then confirm each element's state on the other side: the stepper's arrows may be present-but-disabled-by-data (one item, nothing to step to) rather than extra, and the 'filters' control may be present-but-collapsed or present-in-a-menu in the app rather than missing. 'Absent in this crop' is not 'absent in the design'. If a source comment claims an element 'moved', trust the current rendered reference over the comment. Only once a delta is confirmed by same-width renders of both sides does it get classified (decoration / functionality / owner-approved, migration-parity.md) -- a delta that does not exist has no bucket, and removing the stepper or duplicating a control to fix a non-existent delta is the destructive edit to avoid. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Refuses to remove or add anything based on a one-sided cropped screenshot
Requires rendering both sides at the same viewport width and diffing the corresponding region
Requires confirming element state (disabled-by-data / collapsed / in-a-menu) before calling it extra or missing
Warns the destructive edit would fix a non-existent delta and ties a confirmed delta to the restyle classification

evals.prompt: This repo uses git-flow: features integrate into develop, which is ~40 commits ahead of main. A contributor's large visual-port PR (touching ~30 files) is based on main, not develop. Stage is growth. How do I rate the base?
evals.expected_output: High -- a wrong-base coordination defect, not Medium merge-debt. The PR is built against a product state that no longer exists on the integration line (develop carries ~40 commits main lacks), so merging it into develop will conflict with or revert those commits, and the cost compounds with every commit added on the wrong base -- so the High is intrinsic, and stage (growth here) sets only the urgency to block now, not the severity. Measure and state the divergence -- git rev-list --left-right --count develop...<branch> -- and name the fix in the finding: retarget/rebase onto develop BEFORE more work lands. This sits above the Medium merge-debt row, which is for a long-lived branch diverged from main (a different case). Rating it only 'diverged long-lived branch -> Medium' misses that the base itself is wrong. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Rates the wrong-base as High, not Medium merge-debt
Explains the port is built against a product state absent on the integration line (develop ahead of main)
Requires measuring and stating the left/right divergence count (git rev-list --left-right --count)
Names retarget/rebase onto develop before more work lands as the fix

evals.prompt: We're fanning out a 12-screen restyle to parallel page lanes, each lane restyling one screen. They will all touch the shared layout, nav, and design tokens as needed. Ready to spawn the lanes?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- spawning page lanes onto a shared shell (layout, nav, design tokens, chrome primitives) with no ownership ledger is a High coordination defect: the lanes will edit those shared files concurrently and clobber or silently revert each other's shell changes, invisible in any single lane's diff. Before spawning, publish a shell-ownership ledger (same shape as the fan-out unit manifest): exactly one lane owns each shared-shell path (a partition -- two lanes listing the same path IS the collision), and the shell lands FIRST so page lanes rebase onto the unified chrome rather than a moving one. During review, a page lane's diff that edits a shared-shell path it does not own is a finding even when the diff is correct in isolation, because it diverges the shell the other lanes built on. (migration-parity.md.)

Requires exactly one lane owning each shared-shell path (a partition), reusing the unit-manifest shape
Requires the shell to land first, with page lanes rebasing onto it
Flags a page lane editing an unowned shared-shell path as a finding even when its diff is correct

evals.prompt: Our agent swarm is restyling 12 screens. Plan: each lane opens its own small PR as it finishes, and CI runs the full browser + a11y matrix on every push to every PR. That's 12 PRs, fast to review individually. Good CI plan?
evals.expected_output: No -- 12 fragment PRs each re-triggering the full browser/a11y matrix multiplies shared runner minutes without improving review (the same matrix runs 12 times on work that could review once). Report it ONCE as a cost defect in the fan-out's shape (batched, not one finding per PR), with the staged remedy: prefer one reviewable PR per concern; keep draft iteration on a cheap, path-filtered gate and reserve the browser/a11y matrix for a full-ci label / manual dispatch / the final pre-merge gate; add a concurrency group keyed by PR/ref to cancel superseded runs; keep a one-command local full suite and require the labelled full run before merging an app change. Two hard constraints: path filters must FAIL CLOSED on an unknown path (a filter that skips the gate is a gate exclusion -- a green gate over an unfiltered path is a false pass), and privacy/security checks are never path-filtered out. State the residual risk explicitly -- the cheap gate will NOT catch browser-only regressions until the local or labelled full run, so an unrun matrix is unverified, not a pass. Severity is Medium (recoverable runner cost), not High; only the fail-open filter or a filtered-out security check carries higher severity. (parallel-audit.md.)
expectations: Rejects 12 fragment PRs each triggering the full matrix; reports it once as a batched cost defect, not per-PR

Prescribes the staged pattern: one PR per concern, cheap path-filtered draft gate, browser/a11y reserved for a full-ci label / dispatch / merge gate, concurrency-group cancellation, local full suite plus labelled full run before merge
Requires path filters to fail closed (a skip is a gate exclusion) and never path-filters out privacy/security checks
States the residual risk (cheap gate misses browser-only regressions until the full run; an unrun matrix is unverified) and rates the cost Medium not High

evals.prompt: A restyled entity-detail route: unit tests pass (they assert the pill and label render with the right classes), type-check and lint pass, and a screenshot of the route is attached. Status row: 'route X rendered/verified -- screenshot attached'. In the screenshot, the status pill overlaps the entity's own label at the default width. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: No. A screenshot proves a render happened, not that it is correct -- 'screenshot attached' with no cited inspection is unverified, not verified. The passing unit tests assert the classes render, not where they land; an overlap is geometric and no class assertion catches it. Inspect the image against the pixel-defect checklist and cite what you found: here the OVERLAP item fails -- the status pill intersects the entity label, so the primary text is unreadable at the default width. Report that as a finding (its mechanical proof is a bounding-box non-intersection assertion, testing-and-evals.md). Also name the other items you checked (clip / contrast / disabled-looks-disabled) and which data state the shot is of. A UI status that leans on the image without naming the inspection is an artifact read as the verification it is not. (product-ux-quality.md.)

Reports the overlap as a finding, citing the overlap checklist item
Explains a class assertion cannot catch a geometric overlap; the proof is a bounding-box assertion

evals.prompt: A component test asserts the badge is present and carries the intended utility classes -- it passes. But at the narrow width the badge overlaps its adjacent label. How should the layout be tested, and is the class assertion enough?
evals.expected_output: The class assertion is insufficient evidence for a layout claim -- it only proves the author wrote the class they typed; it passes while the two elements render on top of each other. Overlap is geometric, so the test that counts is a rendered bounding-box non-intersection assertion: read both elements' boundingBox() and assert they do not intersect (and neither collapsed to zero width). Run it at EACH width the project screenshots -- an overlap is width-dependent and usually appears only at the narrow one -- and show it red before / green after the fix. Two companions share the mechanism: clip via scrollWidth > clientWidth, and disabled-looks-disabled via the computed affordance (opacity/cursor), not the attribute. Do NOT assert an absolute pixel position or exact width -- those are renderer- and font-metric-dependent and produce cross-OS flake; the invariant is 'these two do not overlap', never 'this is 132px wide'. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Calls the class assertion insufficient evidence for the layout claim
Prescribes a rendered bounding-box non-intersection assertion, run at each width, red-before/green-after
Names the clip (scrollWidth>clientWidth) and disabled-looks-disabled (computed affordance) companions
Refuses an absolute-pixel/exact-width assertion as the fix (renderer flake); asserts non-intersection only

evals.prompt: A visual port: reference design plus six app routes. So far only the changelog page (static prose, almost no shared chrome) has been rendered and compared -- it matches. Can I report 'the app now matches the design'?
evals.expected_output: No -- that generalizes one verified screen to the whole product. Scope the claim to the rows actually verified: report '1/6 screens verified' and list the five unverified routes; an unrendered screen is an unprobed surface, unverified, not matched (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires). Aggregate phrasing ('the app matches', 'parity achieved') is valid only when every row in the correspondence table reads verified. Cap the verdict below Approve while any in-scope screen is unverified, and carry a 'Parity coverage: 1/6' line in the ground-truth block. Generalizing a sample to the population is a High communication defect -- it retires the verification task and the owner stops checking, then the mismatch surfaces later. Also: the changelog page is the weakest possible sample -- it exercises almost none of the shared shell -- so verify a chrome-bearing, data-dense route next, not another static page. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Refuses 'the app matches the design'; scopes the claim to 1/6 verified and lists the unverified routes
Treats an unrendered screen as unprobed/unverified (coverage kernel); aggregate phrasing valid only when every row is verified
Caps the verdict below Approve and carries a Parity coverage: N/M line; rates the over-generalization a High communication defect
Flags the changelog page as an unrepresentative (shell-less) sample and names a chrome-bearing, data-dense screen to verify next

evals.prompt: Our privacy gate ran in CI and exited 0. The job log shows it scanned for secrets and printed 'clean'. The identifier scan (real names, capital figures on the publish boundary) is driven by a pattern file that is gitignored and absent in CI, so that scan was skipped. Can I mark the publish boundary 'privacy: clean'?
evals.expected_output: No -- a green exit covers only the scopes that actually ran (SKILL.md principle 2: a pass is evidence only where the enforcing surface could see the artifact). The secret scan ran and passed; the identifier scan was SKIPPED because its pattern list was absent, so the identifier surface -- real names and capital figures on the publish boundary -- was never checked. Read which scopes ran, not the bare exit code. 'privacy: clean' here is an over-claim on a trust-critical surface: a real identifier leak would not have been caught. Rate the claim Critical, not the gate. To actually clear the boundary, supply the identifier pattern list (the gitignored .banlist.local.txt or the CI secret that feeds it) and re-run so the identifier scope runs; until then the boundary is unverified for identifiers, and the honest status names the skipped scope. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses 'privacy: clean' when a scope (identifier) was skipped; a pass covers only the scopes that ran
Names the skipped surface as unverified and cites principle 2 (enforcing surface could not see the artifact)
Rates the over-claim Critical as a trust-critical claim, distinguishing the claim from the gate
Requires supplying the pattern list and re-running so the identifier scope actually runs before any clean claim

evals.prompt: A PR that only touches units/ is stuck: the required check 'app-browser' shows no status at all (the job is path-filtered and legitimately didn't run for these paths), and the branch-protection rule won't let it merge. An agent suggested just merging with admin override, or committing an empty change to app/ to make the job run. What's the right call?
evals.expected_output: Treat the missing status as what it is -- a required check with no run for this PR, which blocks merge exactly as a red does and is indistinguishable from a hang; it is not a green pass. Don't fake-trigger it by touching app/ (that ships an unrelated change just to satisfy a gate) and don't reach for admin override as the default (that bypasses the protection for everyone). The real defect is a config gap: a path-filtered job that is also a required check must emit a conclusive status for out-of-scope paths -- a pass-through step that exits 0 -- or the required-check list must not name a job that is legitimately absent for a known class of PRs. Fix the workflow (or the required-check list) so the check is satisfiable, then merge normally. Flag it as a High merge-blocker in its own right, a config gap, not a flake to wait out. The same shape appears when a required job's workflow omits the event that fires the PR (a labeled-only trigger, or a workflow_dispatch run that never attaches to the PR rollup): the workflow existing is not the check running. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: States a required check with no status is not green -- it blocks merge like a failure and is not a pass
Rejects fake-triggering the job with an unrelated change and rejects reflexive admin override as the fix
Identifies the config gap: a path-filtered required check must emit a conclusive status for out-of-scope paths (or not be required for that PR class)
Rates it a High merge-blocker config gap; generalizes to trigger-event gaps (labeled-only, workflow_dispatch rollup)

evals.prompt: Two open PRs both rebuild out/registry.json (a compiled artifact) from source files under units/. Each was branched off main independently and each committed its own rebuilt registry.json. They merge with no conflict. Is that safe?
evals.expected_output: No -- this is the silent-regression case, worse than a conflict. Each PR rebuilt out/registry.json from its OWN base, so each file is valid on its own; git merges both cleanly (no conflict marks), and whichever lands second silently drops the first PR's regeneration -- the first's units/ changes vanish from the compiled artifact with nothing to flag it. The trigger to catch it in review: a PR regenerates a derived artifact (out/, a lockfile, a compiled index, app/data/) AND another open PR touches the same source that produces it -- find the siblings with `gh pr list --state open --limit 500` (the --limit matters; a default page truncates). Fix: the second PR rebases onto the merged first and REBUILDS from the combined source (a superset fold), never layering its own partial build. Flag any generated-artifact PR as superset-fold-required while a sibling source PR is open. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Identifies the silent no-conflict regression: the second merge drops the first's regeneration of the shared artifact
Names the trigger -- a PR regenerating an artifact while another open PR touches the same source -- and finds siblings with gh pr list --limit 500
Requires the second PR to rebase onto the merged first and rebuild from combined source (superset fold), not layer a partial build
Flags generated-artifact PRs as superset-fold-required while a sibling source PR is open

evals.prompt: A follow-up review session. The prior report (captured at SHA a1b2c3) lists a Blocker: a missing authz check at api/orders.ts:88. The branch has since advanced 20 commits. Can I carry that Blocker into the new report as still-open?
evals.expected_output: Not without re-validating it -- a finding carried forward from an earlier SHA without a re-run is a hypothesis, not a confirmed defect. The prior report resolves at its START_SHA (a1b2c3); the tree is now 20 commits ahead, so before repeating the Blocker: (1) re-check that api/orders.ts:88 still exists and still has the gap at HEAD (the line may have moved or the code may be gone), and (2) re-run the gate or probe that surfaced it. Carried forward unchecked it is unverified, not still-open. Two things go wrong if you skip this: the finding may already be FIXED in the 20 commits (repeating it is a false positive that spends the owner's trust), or it may have CHANGED or worsened while you report it unchanged -- reporting a worsened finding as still-open over-claims a trust-critical status; rate that claim, not the staleness. A 'still open' status is only valid at the current SHA -- so record the new report's START_SHA and re-verify each carried finding against it. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses to carry the finding forward as still-open without re-running it; a carried finding without a re-run is a hypothesis (unverified)
Requires re-checking the file:line exists at HEAD AND re-running the surfacing gate before repeating
Names both failure modes: repeating an already-fixed finding (false positive) and reporting a worsened one as unchanged (trust-critical over-claim)
Grounds validity at the current SHA and records the report's start_sha for the next re-verification

evals.prompt: A layout-audit gate that runs against our production build flags a focused control as fully obscured under the sticky header (WCAG focus-not-obscured), at several viewports. I ran the dev server and the control looks fully visible every time -- I can't reproduce it. Is the gate finding a false alarm I can dismiss?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't dismiss a production-build finding because the dev server can't reproduce it. The gate scored the PRODUCTION build (bundled, minified, deployed-style); the dev server is a different artifact -- minification, CSS ordering, hydration timing, and asset paths differ, so a sticky-header overlap real in the built output often does not appear in dev. This is repro fidelity at the ENVIRONMENT axis (the sibling of reproducing with the gate's own detector, and of the local-vs-CI divergence rule): reproduce against the same artifact the gate scored -- build the production bundle and inspect it, or hit the deployed/preview URL -- not the dev server. A dev-server 'looks fine' is unverified against the built surface, not a refutation. Chasing it on the dev server either fixes the wrong tree or dismisses a live accessibility defect. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses to dismiss the production-build finding on a dev-server non-repro; the dev server is a different artifact
Names why they diverge (minification, CSS order, hydration, asset paths) -- the environment axis of reproduction fidelity
Requires reproducing against the same artifact the gate scored (production build or deployed/preview URL)
Treats the dev-server 'looks fine' as unverified against the built surface, not a refutation

evals.prompt: Two open PRs have near-identical titles and both say they fix the same reduced-motion bug -- looks like a clear duplicate. I'm about to close the newer one as a duplicate and merge the older. OK to close it on the title match?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't close a PR as duplicate on title (or branch-name, or same-issue-number) similarity; diff the two heads first, because title similarity is not patch equality. Use two-dot `git diff <tip-A> <tip-B>` when the PRs share a base (the literal difference between the two trees -- empty iff the tips are identical), or `git range-diff <base>..<tip-A> <base>..<tip-B>` to compare the two patch series when they forked from different points (a plain two-dot then pollutes with mainline drift); NOT three-dot `A...B`, which diffs from the merge-base (the `git log` commit-range idiom) and can't isolate what one tip has that the other lacks. The 'duplicate' may carry a hunk the survivor lacks -- e.g. one tip gates a `useReducedMotion` check behind a mount guard (`mounted ? ... : false`) where the other reads it directly. If the newer PR has hunks not in the one you're keeping, FOLD them in first (rebase or cherry-pick), THEN close it with a pointer. Close-as-duplicate is safe only when the diff is empty or the closed PR is a strict subset with no unique lines. Record the diff result in the close comment as the evidence; 'looks the same' is never sufficient, and closing on it silently drops the unique hunk. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Refuses to close-as-duplicate on title/branch/issue-number similarity alone
Requires diffing both PR heads before closing -- two-dot `git diff <tip-A> <tip-B>` for shared-base tips and `git range-diff` for different-base (NOT three-dot, which diffs from the merge-base)
Folds any unique hunks into the survivor first, then closes with a pointer; safe only when the diff is empty or a strict subset
Requires the diff result in the close comment as evidence -- 'looks the same' is insufficient

evals.prompt: PR B absorbed PR A's changes a while ago, so I can merge just B and skip A. But A has a few commits newer than the point B absorbed -- including a fix that disables a submit control. There's no merge conflict between them. Can I merge A then B and be done?
evals.expected_output: No -- merging A then B here silently reverts A's fix. B absorbed A's SOURCE content at an OLDER SHA and is missing A's later commits (the disabled-submit guard); with no textual conflict, B's stale copy of those files overwrites A's fix on merge -- last writer wins and nothing warns. This is distinct from two PRs rebuilding a generated artifact (that's a derived file re-run from source; this is source content absorbed at a stale tip). Fix the order: merge the FULLER tip first and rebase the other onto it, replaying only its unique commits -- or fold A's missing commits into B and merge B once. Then GREP THE LIVE TREE for the fixed symbol (the submit-disable guard); never trust 'B included A.' (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Identifies the silent revert: B absorbed A at an older SHA, so merging B after A overwrites A's later fix with no conflict
Distinguishes it from the generated-artifact superset fold (source content vs a derived rebuild)
Fixes by merge order -- fuller tip first plus a rebase replaying unique commits, or fold A's missing commits into B
Requires a post-merge grep of the live tree for the fixed symbol rather than trusting 'B included A'

evals.prompt: Our main branch is red, and the preflight requires the base green before it will merge anything -- so the three individually-green PRs that would actually fix main can't merge. A teammate wants to just use --admin to force one in. What's the right move?
evals.expected_output: Don't force with --admin -- discharge the deadlock with a merge train. A green-base-required preflight on a red base refuses the very fixes that would green it; that's a deadlock, not a per-PR failure. Union the three individually-green fix PRs on a throwaway integration branch, run the aggregate gate ONCE, and on green merge the members back-to-back (the merge-train procedure) -- the union's green IS the proof the 'base green at head between merges' wait was asking for, so it discharges that wait, which the red base can't otherwise satisfy. The union is a verification vehicle only: don't wait on its CI to hold members that are already green, and never squash/merge the union in place of its members. What the union green does NOT license: merging a red member, an --admin/force-merge past the gate, or an undocumented 'just merge anyway.' A red member is still red; only the base-green-between-merges wait is discharged. Serial-wait between merges only for a true dependency stack that can't share one union, and put the chosen vehicle on the record -- an oral-only exception is itself the finding. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Rejects --admin/force-merge and names the red base plus green-base-required preflight as a deadlock
Prescribes the merge-train discharge: union -> one aggregate gate -> back-to-back member merges; union green discharges the base-green-between-merges wait
Holds the union as verification-only -- not waited on to block already-green members, never merged/squashed in place of members
Bars merging a red member or an oral-only exception; serial wait only for a true dependency stack

evals.prompt: I'm doing a FULL review of a product UI. The diff touched the settings page; I took a headed-browser screenshot of /settings at 390 and 1440, inspected it (no overlap, contrast fine), and I'm ready to call the whole UX review clean. Good?
evals.expected_output: No -- a per-change screenshot of the one route the diff touched is gate 1's receipt, not a FULL UX review. On a FULL review, run the rendered route sweep: enumerate every route from the router tree AND the nav manifest (a route in one but not the other is itself a finding), render each across the matrix -- {~390, ~1440} x {light, dark} x {top, mid-scroll} plus each route's state transitions -- in the running build at the intended base ref, and rule the domain-P checklist on each. Report coverage as a LEDGER, not a verdict: a route you didn't render is unverified, never clean, and a clean finding generalises only to the routes actually rendered, never past them. The defects that reach an owner are the class that spans many routes -- ragged rows, an unpadded sticky bar, an unaxised chart -- which no single-route shot and no green gate ever looked at, so group findings by root cause (a class across many routes is one systemic finding, not forty). (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects a single-route screenshot as a FULL UX review; distinguishes gate 1's per-change receipt from the whole-product sweep
Requires enumerating every route from BOTH the router tree and the nav manifest (a mismatch is itself a finding)
Names the render matrix (viewports x themes x top/mid-scroll x state transitions) in the running build at the base ref
Reports coverage as a ledger -- unrendered routes are unverified not clean, and a clean finding does not generalise past the routes rendered

evals.prompt: Our UX gate screenshots each changed route at 390 and 1440 and asserts no two elements overlap. A sticky filter bar passed -- the shot at the top of the page shows no overlap and clean spacing. Is the sticky bar cleared?
evals.expected_output: Not from a top-of-page shot. The overlap assertion is content-vs-content at the shot's moment; a sticky/fixed-chrome collision happens only once you SCROLL and content passes under the sticky band, and an unpadded sticky bar shows its missing gutter the same way. Both render cleanly at the top of the page at desktop width -- the single condition a casual shot uses -- and are invisible to an overlap/clip check taken there. The sticky-chrome collision and reflow read only mid-scroll or across a state change -- the conditions the rendered route sweep's matrix renders, invisible to a top-of-page shot; gutters and optional-slot reservation read at rest, so they belong on the per-change shot and are re-confirmed in the sweep. The layout invariants beyond overlap/clip are sticky-collision, gutters, optional-slot reservation, no-reflow-on-state-change, and tabular numerals. The sticky collision reuses gate 1's geometry (scroll and sample the header band) and reflow reuses the before/after box compare (the same primitive as overlap), so it is additive, not a new engine -- but the check must run mid-scroll. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Refuses to clear the sticky bar on a top-of-page shot; the collision is visible only mid-scroll
Names the layout invariants beyond overlap/clip (sticky collision, gutters, optional-slot reservation, no reflow on state change, tabular numerals)
Requires checking mid-scroll and on state transitions -- the route sweep's matrix -- not only a fresh top-of-page desktop render
Notes the mechanical half reuses gate 1's primitives (scroll-and-sample, before/after box compare), so it is additive

evals.prompt: A list row exposes its 'archive' action on hover -- it works when I mouse over and click, the handler fires, the row updates. And two buttons of the same kind highlight a bit differently on hover, but both work. Interaction-completeness is satisfied -- fine to ship?
evals.expected_output: Both are defects -- completeness is not consistency. A hover-only action is unreachable on touch and by keyboard: every hover affordance needs a non-hover path (reachable by keyboard focus, present or behind an explicit control on touch), so a mouse-only reveal is a defect, not a power feature -- completeness ('does the control work?') never asks this. The two buttons are an interaction-consistency defect: the same component class must have an IDENTICAL hover/active/focus-visible reaction at every instance; divergent reactions for one class is a finding. Its cause is usually per-instance style overrides on a shared component, so it survives the 'one component per concept' grep (that catches duplicate markup; this catches divergent state styling on the same component) -- enumerate the class's instances and diff their hover/active/focus styles. (frontend-a11y.md owns that a focus ring exists; this owns parity of the reaction across the class.) (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags the hover-only action: every hover affordance needs a keyboard-focus and touch path; completeness does not ask this
Flags the divergent hover as an interaction-consistency defect -- same class must react identically at every instance
Explains it survives the one-component-per-concept grep (divergent state styling on a shared component, not duplicate markup)
Distinguishes from frontend-a11y's focus-ring-exists (this is parity of the reaction across the class)

evals.prompt: A dashboard renders a per-metric trend as a smooth filled area line. The series has three readings this quarter, drawn as a continuous curve so it looks like a clean upward trend. The chart renders cleanly -- no overlap, colours are fine. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: No -- a smooth or filled line drawn across three sparse readings is a fabricated trajectory: it implies values between the measured points that were never sampled, the visual form of principle 4 (empty beats fabricated). Mark each real sample (a dot per reading) and don't smooth or fill across sparse points -- nothing between measured points should be implied. While you're there, rule the rest of the data-viz checklist the clean render hides: a legible value axis (tick labels or direct labels), a keyboard-reachable hover/focus readout returning the value AND its date, and non-visual access to the numbers (a table or aria summary the chart is additive to). 'No overlap, colours fine' is gate 1's inspection, which is structurally blind to chart legibility and to an implied-trend defect. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects the smooth/filled line across sparse samples as an implied (fabricated) trend -- principle 4
Requires marking real samples (a dot per reading) so nothing between measured points is implied
Also rules the chart's legibility: value axis or direct labels, a keyboard-reachable value+date readout, non-visual access to the numbers
Notes gate 1's overlap/colour inspection is structurally blind to chart legibility

evals.prompt: Our dashboard has an 'export chart as PNG' button. The on-screen chart looks great -- axes, a hover readout, correct theme, no clipping, all verified in the running app and green in the gate. The export uses a canvas toDataURL path. Do I need to check the downloaded PNG separately, or does the green on-screen render cover it?
evals.expected_output: Check the downloaded PNG separately -- an export is a SECOND render surface, emitted by a different code path (canvas/toDataURL, SVG serialisation, or an @media print stylesheet) than the screen, so a green on-screen render says nothing about the artifact the user walks away with. Produce the artifact and inspect it like a route: it commonly CLIPS content past the viewport, DROPS the axis/legend/labels and the hover readout that lived only in interactive chrome (chrome rendered outside the serialised root -- an HTML legend or tooltip -- or, for a canvas capture, anything not painted to the bitmap), ignores the current THEME (a light chart exported on a dark page), or exports an empty/partial view as a blank canvas. Rule the domain-P checklist on the PNG itself: no clip, axis/scale/legend/labels baked in (an interactive-only readout needs a static equivalent in the export), theme honored or explicitly normalised, self-describing title/as-of, and every data state exported honestly (never a blank image). Where mechanizable, snapshot the export's dimensions and the presence of its key elements (axis text, legend), held to the could-not-check-vs-found-nothing discipline. This is distinct from verifying which build the reviewer reads (method.md) -- here you inspect an artifact the product emits. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires inspecting the exported artifact separately -- a green on-screen render does not cover the export's different code path
Names the failure modes: clip past the viewport, dropped axis/legend/readout chrome, ignored theme, blank-canvas empty state
Rules the domain-P checklist on the artifact itself (baked-in axes/labels, theme honored/normalised, self-describing, honest data states)
Distinguishes it from reproducing an audit finding against the production build (this inspects an artifact the product emits)

evals.prompt: A review of our app checked every disabled button: they all look disabled (greyed, not-allowed cursor) and the same button class disables the same way everywhere -- appearance and consistency both pass. One is a 'Publish' button disabled until two required fields are filled, but the screen gives no hint why it's off or what to do. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: No -- looking disabled and disabling the same way everywhere are appearance (gate 1's disabled-looks-disabled) and cross-instance consistency (interaction-consistency); neither tells the user WHY the action is unavailable or WHAT unblocks it, and 'Publish is off with no explanation' is a dead end. A contextually unavailable action must name the unmet prerequisite and a concrete next step ('Publish needs a title and a summary', ideally pointing at the empty fields). Crucially, don't put that in the button's own tooltip: a native `disabled` element may receive no hover or focus events, so a tooltip on it is unreachable -- use nearby text or a focusable wrapper/popover the user can actually reach (keyboard included). Separately, an action permanently unavailable to this user's role should be hidden or replaced with an attainable alternative rather than shown as a permanent dead control, unless its discoverability is explicitly wanted. This is the recoverability axis, distinct from appearance and from the disabled-control contrast exemption frontend-a11y.md owns. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Refuses to ship: passing disabled-appearance and consistency does not cover reason + recovery
Requires naming the unmet prerequisite and a concrete next step for a contextually-disabled action
Flags that a tooltip on the disabled element is unreachable (no hover/focus events) -- put the explanation in nearby text or a focusable wrapper/popover
Distinguishes the separate permanent-role case (hidden or replaced with an attainable alternative) from this contextual one

evals.prompt: I delegated a review's fixes to three lanes; each lane reported back 'done' and I compiled the report saying all seven findings are resolved. The owner then asked me to double-check that everything actually landed. I re-read the three lane reports and confirmed each said done -- should I report back that yes, all seven are resolved?
evals.expected_output: No -- re-reading the lane reports re-confirms what they claimed, not what landed; a report of 'done' is not the artifact. Reconcile the seven claims against the COMMITTED DIFF: enumerate the seven as a list and join each to the hunk, test, or file that proves it, marking every one present, partial, or absent, and surfacing your own misses, not only confirming hits. Trust the diff over any lane's say-so -- independent verification (a lead's own read of the code) outranks self-report, and a delegate's 'done' is self-report. And this audit should have run BEFORE you closed, unprompted -- an owner asking 'did you actually do all of it?' is a process incident, the signal the completeness check was owed earlier, not a trigger for it; it is cheap because the claim list and the diff are both already in hand. This set-completeness pass (is every claimed fix present at all) precedes per-claim verification (is each backed by a real surface, not a favorable proxy). (method.md.)
expectations: Rejects re-reading the lane reports as reconciliation -- a 'done' report is not the delivered artifact
Requires enumerating the claim set and joining each claim to the committed diff (hunk/test/file), marking present/partial/absent incl. own misses
Reconciles against the committed diff, not the delegates' reports of what they did
Flags that the audit must run unprompted before close; the owner's challenge is the signal it was owed earlier, and it is cheap

evals.prompt: A redesign made a feed page render only user-posted items, and our test store is kept empty on purpose, so the overlay-open spec that used to run from the feed has nothing to click. We rewrote it to open the overlay from a content-populated page instead; it's green. The comment explains the move. Good to merge?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- the rewrite is correct but it silently drops what the feed spec covered: the overlay could open from the feed, and no test asserts that anymore. A later change that removes the feed's wiring (its import of the shared overlay-link component) would break the feed overlay while the whole suite stays green. Three things are owed before merge: (1) name the retired coverage as a gap -- an unrecorded dropped assertion reads as coverage (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires), and a commit comment is not where coverage is tracked; (2) state that the feed path is now unverifiable via a browser test without seeding the intentionally-empty store, so the gap is a decision, not an accident; (3) add a source-level structural gate -- a unit assertion that the feed component still imports and uses the shared overlay-link component, matching the pattern the codebase's other overlay-wiring tests already use. That fallback is WEAKER than the browser scenario it replaces -- it proves the component is referenced, not that the interaction works -- so it is a named fallback for the retired check, never a substitute that trades rendered coverage for an import check. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Does not pass the rewrite on its new-surface green; flags the silently-dropped feed coverage as a finding
Requires naming the retired coverage as a gap (an unrecorded absence reads as coverage; principle 2), not just a commit comment
Requires a source-level structural fallback that pins the wiring (import/use of the shared component), matching the codebase's existing pattern
States the fallback is weaker than the browser coverage -- pins wiring, not the interaction -- a named fallback, never a substitute

evals.prompt: A static audit lane (browser skipped, memory pressure) reports two gaps with file-level confidence: 'interactive SVG elements have no focus ring -- keyboard users are invisible; build an SVG focus overlay' and 'gaps have no per-item route to land on -- add one.' It grepped for ring-* and for a route segment. Should I brief a lane to build both?
evals.expected_output: No -- not on a static grep. Both are ABSENCE findings, and an absence is unfalsifiable from the report: it claims nothing exists anywhere, but the report can only show what the searcher looked FOR, so anything written in an idiom they didn't try reads as missing. A focus ring can be ring / outline / stroke / box-shadow / a rendered overlay; grepping ring-* alone misses an SVG-native stroke ring (e.g. group-focus-visible:stroke-...). A per-item destination can be a route / query param / hash / id-keyed overlay; a route-segment search misses /issues?focus=<id>. Before any of this becomes a build brief: (a) search by behaviour -- grep every encoding, not one; (b) confirm the absence at RUNTIME (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires) -- render it and look; the browser was skipped, fine for presence checks but not for absence, so these are unverified / unconfirmed-absent, not gaps; (c) if you do brief a lane, instruct it to re-confirm the gap and report back before building, because an absence finding is a work order and a false one builds a second, competing mechanism next to a working one. (method.md.)
expectations: Treats both as absence findings a static grep cannot establish; refuses to authorize construction on them
Requires searching every encoding of the behaviour (ring/outline/stroke/box-shadow/overlay; route/param/hash/id-keyed), not one idiom
Requires runtime confirmation for absence (positive control / principle 2); downgrades unconfirmed absence to unverified, not a gap
A downstream build brief must re-confirm the gap before building -- an absence finding is a work order; a false one builds a competing implementation

evals.prompt: Our audit:ux gate uses scripted focus() at a 320px-tall viewport and reports 26 routes failing keyboard focus. A teammate manually tabbed through at a normal viewport and found 196 clean Tab stops. We've argued for hours over which is right so we can put one 'focus' verdict in the report. Which is correct?
evals.expected_output: Neither is 'wrong,' and there is no single aggregate verdict to report -- these are two different experiments that share the label 'focus.' A behavior claim is only meaningful with the procedure that produced it: scripted focus() vs native Tab is a different INTERACTION METHOD, and 320px-tall vs a full viewport is a different VIEWPORT, and both change what focus does (scripted focus() can land on off-screen or programmatically-focused nodes a Tab sequence never reaches; a short viewport changes what scrolls into view). Two results contradict only when method and viewport match; here they differ, so the honest report preserves BOTH, each labeled with its method + viewport + route coverage (scripted focus() @ 320px: 26 routes fail; native Tab @ full viewport: 196 clean stops), and refuses a flat 'focus passes' or 'focus fails.' To reconcile, run a controlled follow-up that changes one variable at a time (native Tab at 320px; scripted focus() at full height) until the responsible variable is isolated. Both are true experiments, but for the keyboard-USER question the canonical instrument is native Tab (what a real user actually does), not scripted focus(), so once the variable is isolated the native-Tab result is the one that reflects the user's real experience. (report-format.md.)
expectations: Refuses a single aggregate 'focus passes/fails' verdict; preserves both results as method-sensitive, not contradictory
Identifies the differing interaction method (scripted focus() vs native Tab) and viewport (320px vs full) as why both can be true
Requires each claim to carry its method + viewport (+ route coverage) so results are comparable
Reconciles by a controlled follow-up changing one variable at a time, not by declaring a winner

evals.prompt: On our app's home and weekly pages, the Add comment / Submit update / Ask AI buttons render disabled for the first few seconds on a cold load, then go live once the page finishes loading. They read from a client-side useSession hook. A reviewer filed it as a 'disabled control needs an explanation' issue. Is that the right call, and how do we gate it?
evals.expected_output: No -- this is a different class from the contextually-disabled control that owes an explanation. That control STAYS disabled; these WILL enable themselves once the client bundle hydrates and useSession resolves. During the SSR -> hydration window they are in the LOADING data state, so they must LOOK loading -- a skeleton or spinner affordance -- not a bare dead-looking disabled button. The fix is a loading affordance, or optimistic-enabled ONLY if the click is captured and replayed after hydration so the handler is never a no-op; an enabled button whose pre-hydration click is silently dropped is the dead-control / no-op-handler trust defect, not a fix. Gate it as an unverified LEAD, not a finding: the static disabled={!session} pattern with no loading sibling is confirmed only by a pre-hydration render (a snapshot before the client bundle runs); where the harness cannot capture one, report could-not-check and fail open, never a silent pass. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Reclassifies as the LOADING data state during the SSR -> hydration window, not the permanent contextually-disabled class that owes an explanation
Requires a loading affordance (skeleton/spinner) or optimistic-enabled with the click replayed after hydration; a dropped pre-hydration click is the no-op-handler defect
Treats the static disabled={!session} pattern as an unverified lead confirmed only by a pre-hydration render; missing capture is could-not-check / fail-open, not a pass
Does not conflate it with the permanent-disabled-needs-explanation rule

evals.prompt: Our repo's required browser/UX jobs are gated behind a cost label so they don't run on every PR -- the forge reports them SKIPPED/Success, which satisfies branch protection. But our own merge-preflight script refuses to pass any PR where those jobs are SKIPPED if the diff touches app code. An agent can't add the label (owner-only) or trigger the manual dispatch. Local gates are all green. Is the preflight right to hold?
evals.expected_output: No -- the preflight is stricter than the required check it stands in for, and it deadlocks anyone without the owner-only lever. The forge already accepts SKIPPED/Success as green; a local gate that refuses that verdict, whose only unblock is a label or a dispatch the agent is barred from, is a gate stricter than the standard it enforces (the same gate-vs-standard rule product-ux-quality.md / frontend-a11y.md apply to UI) -- a catch-22, not a safety check. The fix is not to weaken the cost gate: it is to make the preflight DIAGNOSE why the job is absent -- policy-declined (the cost gate: work exists, a human must grant the run) vs nothing-to-run (a path filter: no in-scope change) -- and name the owner action, rather than refuse blindly and push the agent toward the forbidden label. Report the local green as the proof it is, flag the config as an agent-unmergeable deadlock (a High config gap, not a flake), and route the run-grant to the owner. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Identifies the local preflight as stricter than the forge's own SKIPPED/Success verdict -- a gate stricter than the standard (gate-vs-standard rule)
Names the deadlock: the only unblock is an owner-only label / dispatch the agent cannot use
Fix is to diagnose policy-declined (cost gate) vs nothing-to-run (path filter) and name the owner action, not to weaken the cost gate or add the label
Treats it as a config gap to route to the owner (High), not a flake to wait out

evals.prompt: A review found a broken auth guard -- disabled={!member} -- on one composer button, where member is briefly undefined so the control dead-ends. We fixed that callsite. Ship the finding as a single-site fix?
evals.expected_output: No -- disabled={!member} is a copyable idiom, so a single callsite is almost never the whole finding. Before calling it single-site, grep the idiom across the tree (the same guard shape, sibling identity flags) in the SAME pass: the search result IS the blast radius, and the finding is reported as one class-finding with its full instance set -- how many sites, and where -- not the first callsite alone. Fixing one and stopping under-scopes the finding and leaks a second fix into a later increment (and a third instance no lane encountered stays broken). This is the review analogue of the one-component-per-concept duplicate-twin sweep (product-ux-quality.md), for a bug pattern rather than a duplicated component: land every instance in one increment, then a single follow-up verifies none remain. (method.md.)
expectations: Refuses the single-site framing; treats the guard as a copyable idiom with a multi-site blast radius
Requires grepping the idiom across the tree in the same pass, the search result defining the instance set
Reports it as one class-finding with its full instance set (count + locations), fixed in one increment
Connects to the duplicate-twin / one-component-per-concept sweep, but for a bug pattern not a duplicated component

evals.prompt: Our LLM review flagged 'user-controlled input reaches this SQL sink -- SQL injection' on one line, and 'the aws-sdk version here is vulnerable' on a dependency. Both sound right. Post them as findings?
evals.expected_output: Not as asserted findings -- corroborate each against the deterministic proof the LLM cannot itself generate, or mark it unverified. 'Input reaches this sink' is a taint/data-flow claim: confirm it against a CodeQL (or equivalent) source->sink path; a claim with no path is unverified, not a finding. 'This version is vulnerable' is an exact version<->CVE match: check osv-scanner / Trivy / Grype against the machine-readable affected-version ranges rather than trusting the model's recall of ranges (error-prone). Running the project's wired scanners is already Phase 1 and re-verifying against source is already the fan-out discipline; this is the security-specific rule that a class a deterministic engine can PROVE is corroborated against that proof (ingested via SARIF / OSV JSON), the LLM layering judgment on top, not asserting the proof. A verified-live secret (TruffleHog Verified) and reachability (Semgrep Supply Chain: importing != executing) are the same pattern. (security-appsec.md.)
expectations: Does not post either claim as a confirmed finding on the model's say-so; corroborates against a deterministic proof or marks unverified
Maps the taint claim to a CodeQL source->sink path and the version claim to an exact OSV/Trivy/Grype version<->CVE match
Names SARIF / OSV JSON as the ingestion format and frames the LLM as layering judgment on a proof it cannot generate
Reuses the existing run-scanners (Phase 1) + re-verify (fan-out) discipline rather than restating it; adds the tool-proof corroboration

evals.prompt: We imprinted our review standards into AGENTS.md so our agents pick them up. But the team also uses Anthropic's managed GitHub Code Review and the local /code-review command, and neither applies our review-specific severity tuning. What should the Phase-6 imprint do?
evals.expected_output: Imprint a review-SCOPED rules block, not just the all-tasks AGENTS.md, and state the surface split. Two consumers read a review-only surface: OpenAI Codex reads a `## Code Review Rules` section of AGENTS.md (root = repo-wide, nested = service-scoped), and Anthropic's MANAGED GitHub Code Review reads a root REVIEW.md (severity recalibration, skip rules, verification bar, nit caps). Map all six severities to the de-facto markers so they agree -- the markers are coarser than the six-level rubric, so map by is-it-a-real-bug (Blocker/Critical/High/Medium -> Important, a Medium is a real defect not a Nit; Low/Nit -> Nit; a pre-existing bug -> Pre-existing). The catch to state in the block: the managed reviewer reads REVIEW.md but the LOCAL /code-review command reads CLAUDE.md ONLY (not REVIEW.md) -- so a rule you need on both goes in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, and REVIEW.md carries managed-only tuning. Same idempotent-additive imprint discipline; author each rule as rule -> bad -> good -> reasoning. (docs-and-dx.md.)
expectations: Adds a review-scoped block (## Code Review Rules in AGENTS.md and/or REVIEW.md), distinct from the all-tasks AGENTS.md context
States the surface split: managed Code Review reads REVIEW.md, local /code-review reads CLAUDE.md only
Maps all six severities to the de-facto markers, Medium -> Important (a real defect, not a Nit), Low/Nit -> Nit, pre-existing -> Pre-existing
Keeps the idempotent-additive imprint discipline and the rule->bad->good->reasoning format
